title: Tuscany
description: Hills, cypresses and Sangiovese: Chianti, Brunello and the Super Tuscans that rewrote Italian law.
L: Hills between Florence and the sea

Tuscany, in central Italy, stretches from the Apennines in the east to the Tyrrhenian Sea in the west. Most vineyards are on hills between 150 and 600 m, among olive groves and cypresses. The heart is Chianti, between Florence and Siena. South are Montalcino and Montepulciano; on the coast, Bolgheri and the Maremma.

Tuscany has a Mediterranean climate: hot, dry summers and mild winters. Inland, altitude and hills bring cool nights that preserve acidity. The coast is warmer, with sea breezes. Soils include galestro, a crumbly schist-like marl, and alberese, a hard limestone, both prized for Sangiovese.
Which soils are prized for Sangiovese in Tuscany?
Galestro marl and alberese limestone give fine Sangiovese.

The Etruscans made wine here before the Romans. In 1716, Cosimo III de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany, defined the boundaries of Chianti, Carmignano, Pomino and Valdarno, one of the earliest legal wine regions. In the 1870s, Baron Bettino Ricasoli set a Chianti formula led by Sangiovese.
Yes, by Cosimo III de' Medici.
Tuscany runs from the Apennines to the sea
Hills and altitude cool its Mediterranean climate

Sangiovese is Tuscany's grape: sour cherry, herbs and earth, high acidity and firm, tea-like tannin. It has local names and clones: Brunello in Montalcino, Prugnolo Gentile in Montepulciano, Morellino in Scansano. Native partners include Canaiolo, Colorino and Mammolo.

Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Syrah arrived in the 20th century, especially on the coast in Bolgheri. They're used in Super Tuscans and allowed in small amounts in Chianti Classico. White grapes include Vernaccia di San Gimignano, Tuscany's oldest DOCG white, Vermentino on the coast, and Trebbiano and Malvasia for Vin Santo.
Match each name to its place.
Vin Santo, Tuscany's sweet wine from dried Trebbiano and Malvasia, is served with cantucci almond biscuits.
Sangiovese leads, with local names like Brunello
Bordeaux grapes thrive on the coast
Vernaccia, Vermentino and Vin Santo complete the whites

Chianti Classico DOCG covers the original zone between Florence and Siena, with villages like Greve, Radda, Gaiole and Castellina. Its symbol is the black rooster, gallo nero. It must be at least 80% Sangiovese, with native or international grapes for the rest; white grapes were banned in 2006.

Chianti Classico has three levels: Annata, at least 12 months' ageing; Riserva, 24 months; and Gran Selezione, introduced in 2014, from estate grapes, at least 30 months and, since 2021, at least 90% Sangiovese. Since 2021, labels can name 11 UGAs, Unità Geografiche Aggiuntive, villages like Panzano and Radda.
Order these Chianti wines by minimum ageing, shortest first.
Plain Chianti is a separate, broader DOCG with lower requirements; Gran Selezione is the top.

Chianti DOCG is a separate, much larger area surrounding Chianti Classico, with seven sub-zones like Chianti Rufina and Colli Senesi. Rules are looser: at least 70% Sangiovese. Quality varies, from simple to excellent; Rufina, in the cool hills east of Florence, is often the best.
What is the symbol of Chianti Classico?
Chianti Classico is the historic heart, at least 80% Sangiovese
Annata, Riserva and Gran Selezione are its levels
Chianti DOCG is broader, with seven sub-zones

Montalcino, a hill town about 40 km south of Siena, is warmer and drier than Chianti. Brunello di Montalcino, DOCG since 1980, must be 100% Sangiovese, aged at least five years, two in oak; Riserva six years. The Biondi-Santi family created it in the late 19th century. Rosso di Montalcino is a younger, lighter version.

Montepulciano, east of Montalcino, makes Vino Nobile di Montepulciano DOCG from at least 70% Sangiovese, here called Prugnolo Gentile, aged at least two years. It's often softer than Brunello and more structured than Chianti. Since 2021, Pieve, a top tier from defined sub-areas, has been introduced.
Match each wine to its rule.
Each Tuscan red has its own rules.
Don't confuse Vino Nobile di Montepulciano, a Tuscan Sangiovese, with Montepulciano d'Abruzzo, a different grape from another region.
Brunello is 100% Sangiovese, aged five years
Vino Nobile is at least 70% Prugnolo Gentile
Montalcino is warmer and drier than Chianti

In the 1960s and 1970s, Chianti rules forced producers to include white grapes and limited new ideas. Some made wine their own way: Sassicaia, from Cabernet Sauvignon at Bolgheri, first sold in 1971; Tignanello, from Antinori, in 1971, a Sangiovese and Cabernet blend in small barrels. Sold as simple table wine, they cost more than any Chianti.

Bolgheri, on the coast, has gravelly soils and a warm, maritime climate, with sea breezes, close to Bordeaux's conditions. Bordeaux grapes thrive: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc. Ornellaia, Masseto and Sassicaia are its icons. Bolgheri DOC came in 1994; Sassicaia got its own DOC, Bolgheri Sassicaia, in 2013, the only single-estate DOC in Italy.
It was Cabernet Sauvignon sold as table wine
A Cabernet from the coast, outside DOC rules.

The Super Tuscans' success led Italy to create the IGT category, Indicazione Geografica Tipica, in 1992, for quality wines outside DOC rules. Toscana IGT now includes many top wines. Chianti Classico's rules also changed, allowing 100% Sangiovese and some international grapes.
Super Tuscans broke DOC rules in the 1970s
Bolgheri's coastal gravel suits Bordeaux grapes
Reading Tuscany and eating with it

Labels show the DOCG, like Chianti Classico, Brunello di Montalcino or Vino Nobile, or Toscana IGT for Super Tuscans, plus producer, vintage and sometimes Riserva, Gran Selezione or a UGA. The pink DOCG neck strip and, for Chianti Classico, the black rooster confirm origin.

Sangiovese's acidity loves tomato and olive oil: pasta with tomato sauce, pappardelle with wild boar ragù, ribollita, a bread and bean soup, and bistecca alla fiorentina, a thick grilled T-bone. Brunello suits game and aged pecorino. Vernaccia and Vermentino suit seafood. Vin Santo suits cantucci.
Which dish is a Tuscan classic with Chianti Classico or Brunello?
Serve Tuscan reds at 16 to 18 degrees. Chianti Classico Annata is best within five years; Riserva and Gran Selezione 10 to 20; Brunello 15 to 30. Decant young Brunello and Super Tuscans.
Chocolate mousse needs a sweet wine.
